THOUGHT: This 60-year-old woman presents with sudden, painless, unilateral vision loss—specifically no perception of light (NLP) in the right eye—onset ~30 minutes prior. Key ophthalmic findings include an afferent pupillary defect (absent direct light reflex in the affected eye with preserved consensual response), normal intraocular pressure, and fundoscopic findings of a pale, whitened retina with a cherry-red spot at the macula — the classic triad of central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO). The cherry-red spot arises because the macula is relatively thin and overlying the choroidal circulation, which remains visible while the surrounding retina becomes ischemic and opaque due to retinal arterial obstruction. Her vascular risk profile is highly relevant: age >60, hypertension, diabetes, coronary artery disease, smoking, and poor medication adherence — all strongly predispose to atherosclerosis and embolic or thrombotic events. CRAO is typically embolic (e.g., from carotid plaque or atrial fibrillation), though in situ thrombosis can occur in setting of severe vasculopathy (e.g., diabetic or hypertensive retinopathy). The absence of pain, normal IOP, and lack of optic disc swelling acutely help distinguish CRAO from other causes: angle-closure glaucoma (painful, elevated IOP), optic neuritis (usually painful, often with relative afferent pupillary defect but normal fundus early on), ischemic optic neuropathy (disc edema, no cherry-red spot), and retinal detachment (often with floaters/flashes, visual field defect but not NLP unless total, and fundus shows elevation/shadowing). Given the acute onset, painless nature, NLP, afferent pupillary defect, and pathognomonic fundus appearance, CRAO is the most likely diagnosis. Time is critical — irreversible retinal infarction begins within 90–240 minutes; this qualifies as a true ophthalmologic emergency requiring immediate intervention.

DIAGNOSIS: Central retinal artery occlusion
